verdicts.summary: Lean has an equivalent formula. The Lean states the same two conservative forms without the r² and r weights, and without assuming axisymmetry or incompressibility; the rewriting is a term-by-term multiplication. Set dtheta ≡ 0 (axisymmetric) and divergence w = 0, so `conservativeAngular_eq` reads conservativeAngular = residualAngular = ℛ_θ. Multiplying by r²: r²∂_t u_θ = ∂_t(r²u_θ); r²[∂_r(u_ru_θ) + (2/r)u_ru_θ] = ∂_r(r²u_ru_θ) (this is why the weight 2 appears in `radialDivergence 2`); r²∂_z(u_zu_θ) = ∂_z(r²u_zu_θ); -r²∂_zz u_θ = -∂_zz(r²u_θ); and -r²[∂_rr u_θ + ∂_r u_θ/r] + u_θ = -∂_r(r²∂_r u_θ - r u_θ), which is where Lean's Bessel term + w 1 / radius² goes. Likewise r·conservativeAxial: r[∂_r(u_ru_z) + u_ru_z/r] = ∂_r(r u_r u_z), r[∂_z(u_z²) + ∂_z p] = ∂_z(r(u_z²+p)) since r does not depend on z, and -r[∂_rr u_z + ∂_r u_z/r] = -∂_r(r∂_r u_z). Lean is more general than the paper's 'smooth axisymmetric divergence-free field': it keeps the θ-derivatives and carries the exact correction u_i·div u instead of assuming div u = 0. The r-weighted form itself is not a Lean declaration; in profile (R) coordinates the weighted densities used for the moment argument are SlowStressSupport.angularDensity / axialDensity, which I read but did not match term by term to this physical display.
